name: Glypromate
lead: Glypromate, also called GPE (glycine-proline-glutamate), is a tripeptide that corresponds to the N-terminal fragment of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). It is an endogenous peptide found in the brain and described as having anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties in laboratory research [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and peptide discussions it belongs to the group of IGF-1-related peptides, whose appeal is the growth, recovery and tissue-quality effects associated with the IGF-1 axis; no source documents GPE itself being used for appearance.

The IGF-1 connection is concrete: des(1-3)IGF-I is a truncated IGF-1 variant that lacks exactly this Gly-Pro-Glu tripeptide, isolated from bovine colostrum, human brain and porcine uterus. It binds IGF-binding proteins much less and is roughly ten-fold more potent than IGF-1 at stimulating hypertrophy and proliferation of cultured cells, with selective anabolic effects in gut tissue when given to animals [3].

The natural tripeptide crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and is broken down quickly, so researchers have developed more than 100 analogues; the best known is trofinetide, approved in 2023 for Rett syndrome [2][4]. Glypromate itself was the subject of a randomised trial aimed at preventing cognitive deficits after cardiac surgery [5].

angle.text: People interested in IGF-1-related peptides discuss GPE as a fragment of that system. The documented research concerns brain protection, so any link to physique or skin is an extrapolation by enthusiasts rather than a studied outcome.

paras: Wikipedia describes GPE as a cleavage product of IGF-1 with neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, listing Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease among the areas of research interest. Its reference list indicates that scientific papers on GPE and the CNS date back to at least 1993, and that reviews of GPE and its derivatives as neuroprotective agents appeared in 2009, 2012 and 2023 [1].

A 2023 review describes GPE as holding promise for neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease and for Rett and Down's syndromes, and says its limited pharmacokinetic properties hinder clinical application, which has driven work on more than 100 analogues over two decades [2].

Because the native peptide is unstable, work has concentrated on derivatives. NNZ-2566, an alpha-methylated analogue with an improved elimination half-life, showed neuroprotective efficacy in a rat model of stroke [6]. Trofinetide, a modified GPE analogue developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals, was approved by the US FDA in March 2023 for Rett syndrome [4]. Newer work examines conjugates of glypromate with bioactive amines [7], and safety studies have looked at the toxicity of pseudotripeptide derivatives in cells and embryos [8].

Glypromate has been studied in a randomised controlled trial for neuroprotection during cardiac surgery; a 2009 review noted that its results were not yet known when written [5]. No studies of glypromate for appearance were found. Human trials exist for its analogue trofinetide in Rett syndrome and Fragile X syndrome [4].

card.summary: The IGF-1-derived tripeptide GPE, a neuroprotection research compound whose analogue trofinetide became an approved Rett syndrome drug.
card.note: Experimental; no human trials of the unmodified peptide located.

quick.overview:
Glypromate is a three-amino-acid piece of IGF-1. In lab research it has been examined as a neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory agent.

It is chiefly of interest as the parent of trofinetide. Nothing in the sources reviewed links it to a documented appearance benefit.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to act in brain tissue as a neuroprotective signal derived from IGF-1; because the plain peptide is rapidly degraded, more stable analogues were developed.[1]
quick.risks: Experimental and not approved. No human safety data for the unmodified peptide were found in the sources reviewed.
